headings.title: Introduction to Adolescent Nutrition and Growth Spurts
headings.content: Adolescence represents a critical transitional phase characterized by rapid physical growth, psychological maturation, and shifting social dynamics. During this phase, individuals experience a major growth spurt, second only to infancy in terms of velocity. This pubertal growth spurt involves profound skeletal, muscular, and hormonal changes, leading to increased nutritional demands. For nursing students in Nigeria, understanding adolescent nutrition is vital because inadequate dietary intake during these formative years can stunt final adult height, delay sexual maturation, and compromise long-term health outcomes. Girls typically experience their growth spurt earlier than boys, around age 10 to 12, while boys usually peak around age 12 to 14. These rapid changes mean that the body requires a high influx of energy and specific building blocks to support expanding blood volume, increasing lean body mass, and bone mineralization. Nutritional requirements are therefore proportionally higher per unit of body weight during adolescence than at almost any other time in the lifecycle. Nurses play a crucial educational role in guiding adolescents and their families through this physiological transition, ensuring that traditional and modern dietary patterns provide sufficient energy and nutrients to meet these heightened metabolic demands.

headings.title: Macronutrient and Micronutrient Requirements in Adolescence
headings.content: Meeting the nutritional demands of adolescence requires a careful balance of both macronutrients and micronutrients. Macronutrients—carbohydrates, proteins, and fats—provide the necessary energy and structural elements for growth. Protein intake is especially crucial during the pubertal growth spurt to support the expansion of lean body mass, organ growth, and skeletal muscle development. Carbohydrates should form the bulk of energy intake, prioritizing whole grains and complex sources over refined sugars to maintain steady energy levels and metabolic health. Healthy fats are also necessary for brain development and hormone production. Beyond macronutrients, micronutrients take center stage due to the rapid remodeling of tissues. Calcium and vitamin D are indispensable for maximizing peak bone mass, which helps prevent osteoporosis later in life, particularly since nearly half of adult skeletal mass is formed during adolescence. Iron needs surge to support the expanding blood volume in both sexes, as well as to replace menstrual losses in adolescent girls. Zinc is another vital micronutrient required for cellular growth, sexual maturation, and immune function. Nigerian nursing professionals must assess local dietary staples to ensure adolescents receive adequate quantities of these essential nutrients, preventing deficiencies that can impair academic performance and physical stamina.

headings.title: Nutritional Assessment and Anthropometric Measurement in Youth
headings.content: Nutritional assessment is a systematic process used by nurses to evaluate the nutritional status of adolescents and identify risks of malnutrition, whether undernutrition or overnutrition. The core components of this assessment include anthropometric measurements, biochemical tests, clinical evaluations, and dietary history. Anthropometry involves non-invasive, quantitative measurements of the body, notably height, weight, and Body Mass Index (BMI). In adolescents, plotting weight and height on age- and sex-specific growth charts—such as those provided by the World Health Organization (WHO)—is critical because growth patterns vary drastically compared to adults. A BMI-for-age percentile helps classify adolescents into categories such as underweight, healthy weight, overweight, or obese. Nurses must accurately measure height using a stadiometer and weight using a calibrated scale, ensuring proper positioning. Additionally, measuring mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) can be useful in resource-constrained settings to quickly screen for acute malnutrition. Beyond physical measurements, clinical observations such as skin pallor, brittle hair, or dental caries offer physical clues regarding nutrient deficiencies, guiding the nurse toward appropriate dietary interventions and referrals.

headings.title: Common Nutritional Deficiencies: Anemia and Micronutrient Gaps
headings.content: Adolescents are particularly vulnerable to specific nutritional deficiencies, with iron-deficiency anemia standing out as a major public health concern globally and within Nigeria. Anemia results from insufficient iron to form adequate hemoglobin, leading to fatigue, reduced cognitive function, poor concentration, and lowered physical endurance, which can severely impact academic performance. Adolescent girls face a heightened risk due to the onset of menstruation combined with inadequate dietary iron intake from plant-based staples that may have low bioavailability. Other micronutrient gaps commonly observed include vitamin A deficiency, which impairs immunity and vision, iodine deficiency affecting cognitive development, and folate deficiency. Nurses must recognize the clinical signs of anemia, such as conjunctival pallor, lethargy, and shortness of breath during exertion. Combating these deficiencies involves promoting dietary diversification, encouraging the consumption of heme iron sources (such as lean meats and fish) alongside vitamin C-enhanced plant sources to boost absorption, and supporting national micronutrient supplementation and food fortification programs, such as iron-folic acid distribution for school-age girls.

headings.title: Eating Disorders and Body Image Issues in Adolescents
headings.content: Adolescence is a vulnerable period for the development of eating disorders and distorted body image issues. Physical changes during puberty, coupled with societal pressures, media influence, and peer comparisons, often trigger intense dissatisfaction with body weight and shape. Conditions such as anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, and binge-eating disorder typically emerge or peak during the adolescent years. Anorexia nervosa is characterized by severe caloric restriction, an intense fear of gaining weight, and a distorted body image, leading to dangerous emaciation. Bulimia nervosa involves recurrent episodes of binge eating followed by inappropriate compensatory behaviors such as self-induced vomiting, fasting, or excessive exercise. Nurses must remain vigilant for behavioral and physical warning signs, including dramatic weight loss, preoccupation with calories, wearing baggy clothes to hide weight loss, frequent trips to the bathroom after meals, dental enamel erosion, and electrolyte imbalances. Management requires a multidisciplinary approach involving medical stabilization, psychological counseling, and specialized nutritional rehabilitation. Nurses provide compassionate, non-judgmental support, fostering a positive self-esteem and healthy relationship with food among youths.

headings.title: Adolescent Obesity and Metabolic Health Risks
headings.content: Conversely, adolescent obesity has emerged as a major global health epidemic, driven by the nutritional transition toward energy-dense, highly processed foods, sugary beverages, and increasingly sedentary lifestyles characterized by screen time and reduced physical activity. Childhood and adolescent obesity carries severe metabolic health risks that often track into adulthood, including type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), and psychosocial complications such as low self-esteem and depression. Excess adiposity during youth can cause premature vascular changes and metabolic syndrome. Nurses play a crucial role in screening for obesity using BMI-for-age percentiles and identifying early metabolic markers. Interventions focus on family-centered lifestyle modifications rather than restrictive diets that could trigger eating disorders. Nurses educate adolescents and their families on portion control, reducing sugar-sweetened beverage consumption, increasing whole foods, fiber, and fruits, and incorporating regular physical activity into daily routines. Advocacy for school health policies that promote physical education and restrict junk food sales is also an important nursing responsibility in combating adolescent obesity.

headings.title: Nutritional Needs of Pregnant and Parenting Adolescents
headings.content: Adolescent pregnancy presents unique and complex nutritional challenges because the pregnant teen has competing physiological demands: she is still growing and developing herself while simultaneously nourishing a growing fetus. This dual demand increases the risk of maternal complications such as anemia, pregnancy-induced hypertension, and cephalopelvic disproportion, as well as infant complications including low birth weight, preterm birth, and intrauterine growth restriction. Pregnant adolescents require higher caloric, protein, calcium, and iron intakes compared to adult pregnant women to support their own ongoing skeletal growth alongside fetal development. Furthermore, parenting adolescents face ongoing nutritional vulnerabilities as they juggle infant care, financial constraints, and their own nutritional restoration postpartum, especially if they choose to breastfeed. Nurses working in maternal and child health settings must provide intensive nutritional counseling, ensure timely antenatal care attendance, and facilitate access to nutrient supplementation programs such as iron and folic acid tablets. Emphasizing weight gain monitoring and promoting nutrient-dense local foods helps safeguard both the young mother's health and the optimal growth of her child.

headings.title: Nursing Interventions, Counseling, and Dietary Education
headings.content: Nursing interventions, counseling, and dietary education are cornerstone strategies for promoting optimal nutritional health among adolescents. Nurses interact with youth in diverse settings, including schools, community clinics, outpatient departments, and youth centers, making them ideally positioned to deliver targeted health promotion. Effective nutritional counseling requires a non-judgmental, empathetic, and culturally sensitive approach that respects adolescent autonomy while involving families when appropriate. Motivational interviewing is a valuable communication technique nurses use to help adolescents explore their ambivalence about changing unhealthy dietary habits and set achievable personal goals. Dietary education should be practical, focusing on how to make healthier food choices within local economic and cultural contexts, such as selecting nutritious Nigerian foods over empty-calorie processed snacks. Nurses must also assess food security at the household level, collaborate with interprofessional teams including dietitians and social workers, and advocate for school-based nutrition programs. By empowering adolescents with knowledge about balanced nutrition, portion control, and the risks of fad diets, nurses lay the foundation for lifelong healthy eating habits.
